title: 12 Angry Men
comment: I remember watching this movie on one my last lessons in Legal Studies in Australia because there's not much else to do besides the exam prep. I don't understand the appeal of this movie at all. All it is revolves around twelve angry men yelling at each other for the entire movie, in one room. Sure, it tells the story (and I'm seriously stretching the term for this particular live action reel) of a jury made up of 12 men as they deliberate the guilt or acquittal of a defendant on the basis of reasonable doubt, forcing the jurors to question their morals and values. This works well as a play and I like the acting and dialogue in this, but does not translate well onto movie at all. That's what Parliament Question Time TV show is there for. This movie is so boring, forgettable and torturous that this is the third time I literally fell asleep a half hour in besides Transformers: Age of Extinction and the new version of Independence Day. Because movies are meant to entertain people, even Tommy Wisseau's The Room and the animated Titanic movies are watchable compared to this torture device. This movie is generally studied in English (lucky I never had to do that, even though there was no way I could escape seeing this movie), and I feel for the high school students who have to watch this for study, and fans of this movie who would throw their money at everything they see.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
First thing the defendant was guilty in "12 Angry Men,". However, this movie exposes the huge flaws in the jury system. Even when evidence and testimony supports a guilty verdict a single self-righteous bully swayed the decisions of other jurors,

Juror 8 is portrayed as a champion of justice, but his methods of jury tampering by introducing an identical knife and speculating on witness testimonies, steps beyond courtroom protocols. He dismisses the old man's account and makes assumptions about the female witness's eyesight all based on personal experiments and conjecture, not verified evidence.

Juror 8's tactics and amateur detective work, created bias on the jury with emotional appeals rather than sticking to the trial facts, and undermining the judicial process. Thank goodness this movie is a fictional, account using dramatic license, and should not be taken as a real case study.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
12 Angry Men is a pretentious amateur "detective" story who's manipulative intent was easy to spot a mile away. As soon as they showed Henry Fonda's character of the The Architect (Juror # 8) I knew he was going to be the only one emotional enough to vote not guilty and with the help of very poor writing convince everyone else to do the same. Sure enough I was right.

Juror # 8 starts off just believing the 19-year old suspect was abused by his father for "years" with absolutely no evidence other than his bleeding heart and not simply disciplined for all the crimes he committed which included mugging, auto theft, robbery and knife fighting because as we know no one ever lies except of course all the eye witnesses in this trial and the detectives.

The Architect just makes one nonsense argument after another and every valid point brought up by the skeptics is just brushed aside until they finally change their mind for no logical reasoning whatsoever.

For instance, juror # 8 just manufacturers a time frame with no evidence to support it about how long it takes elevated train cars to pass by a single point. He does this based on his alleged past experience of living in an apartment near an elevated train line and everyone just buys it with no argument. This is embarrassingly bad for a number of reasons;

Since the film is set in New York City around 1956-57 we can find that during this time period there were 3 distinct elevated train car types (MUDC, Q-CARS and LO-V) from 7 different manufacturers (ACF, Cincinnati, IRT, Jewett, Pullman St. Louis, Wason) operating. It is just assumed in the film that every elevated train in NYC is made up of identical length, height and speed trains with the exact same window dimensions and placement when nothing could be farther from the truth.

What year did Juror # 8 have this apartment and what exact trains were running on the line at that time? Were those the same type's of train cars involved in this case? No answer is given. This is the equivalent of saying that you flew out of an airport years ago therefore all planes are the same and fly at the same speed with no control by the pilot.

Trains are operated by conductors and are variable speed, they speed up and slow down. At any given day a conductor could be running a train faster or slower for any number of reasons. They could be trying to make up time being late and running the train faster, they could have been tired and running the train slower to be safe or any number of other variables. There is no way to know the exact timing of the train that day unless you were there to time it.

Then the old man juror becomes an amateur criminal profiler and accuses the old man witness of lying to be important with no actual evidence to support this just his worthless opinion based on how he looks.

A juror not remembering the details of a movie is not an argument. The day a family member of mine died I have the movie I was watching seared into my head and will never forgot it. During times of increased stress like this you become hyper aware of everything.

The entire debate over how the suspect would have stabbed his dad is waste of time, all that matters was if it was plausible. How a juror would hold the knife is irrelevant.

Apparently the jurors have never heard of reading glasses or sunglasses which first became popular in the 1920's and The Stockbroker (Juror # 4) just decides to become an idiot on this point for no reason.

This is a manipulative and poorly written film designed to sow doubt where none exists and to instead have you believe in emotional reasoning over logic.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
As a team of film critics, we recently went to the cinema to see a broadcast of the movie "12 angry men" and God, what a great film for octogenarians! Maybe to give you our opinion about it, we must put this dud into context.

12 angry men or "12 hommes en colère" in French, is a 1957 American courtroom drama film directed by Sidney Lumet and based on the eponymous piece of theatre of 1954 written by Reginald Rose. As Lumet is a filmmaker known for his tragedies and critics of American justice system, we were, as fans waiting for a harrowing masterpiece! But we think that our small introduction made you understand that we were disappointed.

The movie unfolds in a jury room in which 12 jurors are deliberating the case of an impoverished 18-year-old boy who is accused of stabbing his father to death. Therefore, the spectator follows this uneven trial for not less than ninety-six minutes, which is of course a bit exhausting. However, you may be pleased when seeing the cast with Henry Fonda, which would be normal. Yet, he probably is the reason of the movie's recognition, because there is nothing else that distinguishes it from other courtroom films such as Liar Liar from 1997. Maybe, we are scandalmongers because you probably know Martin Balsam? Or John Fiedler? No, you don't? To be honest we think that Fonda, Mr Davis in the movie, or the juror eight truly makes the film. If the gamechanger, the one who was about to save the young boy by rebelling against the tyranny of the majority, was anonymous for the spectators, would people give the movie that much attention? We do not think so. Nevertheless, the themes addressed in this film seemed intrusting: the justice and the question of morality and values are omnipresent, but they would be the few positive points. In fact, it contains an underlying message about prejudicial actions, the difficulties to be a juror and even racism during the fifties. It provides an interesting perspective on the importance of being a juror and the possible biases that jurors could, and still can encounter nowadays. It is both dramatic and tense, and it is insightful in its depiction of various aspects of humanity. But we were unable to identify with this film as it was impossible to identify with any of the jurors, it felt like they were not communicating any emotion.

Moreover, the script may seem ingenious but if you dig a bit it is not really the case and almost becomes boring at one point. It was so hard not to fall asleep while watching it. We were neither surprised nor excited to see the film and after we saw it. Don't you think the story is a bit far-fetched? Twelve brains take ninety minutes to agree on such an obvious case? Of course, he was not guilty. But after all, this movie kind of shows how screwed up the American justice system is. The poor boy is found guilty before all the evidence were even considered. Logic would dictate that he is not guilty until proven innocent, but apparently only one brain managed to take that detail into account, which made the scenario a bit inconceivable.

To be the most objective as possible, 12 angry men is one of the films that did not aged well. Overall, this is a good movie if you like vintage (because it is trending again), slow-paced, and closed-door films. You can also go see it if you like films that denounce timeless issues that still occur today. Also, if you like Henry Fonda, you want to watch it because he still plays greatly. It can be a great old school classic, but definitely a waste of time for people, like us from Generation Z. If you are into more dynamic courtroom movies, we would advice you to watch more recent ones, such as "Just mercy" from 2019 or "the Trial of the Chicago 7" that was released last year!

title: 12 Angry Men
comment: I have tried, and tried again to like this film. But I fail after the first fifteen minutes. For a start it is a Henry Fonda vehicle based on a television play. And sadly it still looks like and feels like a television play. The line up of actors like Ed Begley, Lee J. Cobb etc is impressive and they act well if over theatrically. Fonda is Fonda and I repeat he is the star and he does his best to shrug off his usual coldness on film. I have nothing against his acting except that I do not respond to his way of performing. A little more warmth, and being less dour I would perhaps, and it is a big perhaps, to respond to him better. So this for me is one of the fault lines in the film and his stabbing a knife on the table is a great moment. Being a big star the moment has tremendous impact, and no doubt most audiences are caught. As for the plot of the film it is about a youth who has to all intents committed a murder and twelve jurors debate about his going to the electric chair or not. I know it was 1957 and just maybe it was too daring to ask but no one questions capital punishment in itself, and twelve angry men could dispute that in itself but of course it is not on the table. The film is often praised for its camera movements, claustrophobic towards the end and less so at the beginning. The only unintended humour for me was one of the more elderly men taking too long in the toilet. Or bathroom in ' respectable ' terms and the latter is of course used. No spoilers to the ending. But with signposts all the way a child could work it out. I also have not read in any reviews of this ' great ' film that the jurors are all baying for blood, and to get out of the room on a hot day as soon as possible. My opinion is I know a minority one, but for me the film does not dare to even question the biggest of all basic and human issues and that is if capital punishment is right or wrong in itself.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment: "12 Angry Men" (1957), I have heard people go nuts over this "film", time and time again. The hype was insane between everyone I've heard who mentioned anything about it or anything related to it. So, I finally gave in and put it on. What a major disappointment! It is, without a shadow of a doubt, one of the top 10 most boring films I've ever seen in my life. I've seen a lot of dull and boring movies, but this "film" excels at both of those aspects. This "movie" has a boring story, standard to horrible acting and a generic dull soundtrack. As far as the story goes, it's one of the most uninteresting, boring, unnecessary and unbearable I've ever seen. It's only 96 minutes, but it felt like I was watching it for days! The storyline is, 12 jurors argue on whether a person is guilty or not guilty. Seriously, that's the whole movie, just 12 boring characters sitting in a boring room talking. How riveting! Right? You might as well hide a couple of video cameras in a jury room and press record, same thing! Now, I have seen movies before that take place in a single setting from beginning to end. Some were good, some were bad. "12 Angry Men" is probably one of the worst examples of how not to make a film taking place in the same location. It was so dull, that I could barely fight to keep my eyes open! Another big issue is lack of character development. The main characters are cast as: Juror 1, Juror 2, etc. Yes, we do find out their names at the end when they introduce themselves. That's one of the biggest cardinal rules when making a movie or TV show, character development. This "movie" has virtually none of that. The only positive about this "film" is that it somehow inspired a lot of tributes and parodies on TV shows. Those were so much more entertaining than this pile of filth! Before you guys tell me, "it's realistic, this movie is supposed to be as close to a real-life scenario as possible." I'm all for movies with realism. When done right, it can be very effective! "12 Angry Men" is a little bit too real. Wow, I never thought I'd hear myself say that! Overall, the plot of this "movie" is so bad, that describing my feelings toward it as angry is an understatement. That's one of the two worst things a film can do; anger me, or bore me. "12 Angry Men" does both! As far as the acting goes, it's just as bad, unfortunately. From the whole entire cast! The only ones who actually seem to be trying are Henry Fonda, E.G. Marshall, Martin Balsam and Jack Warden. All of the rest of the performances were either bad or just plain boring. It's a real pity, because all of these actors are great in other movies and TV shows. What happened here? Finally, the soundtrack in this "movie" is overall very generic and not memorable in the least. There are a couple of parts of the film score that aren't too bad. The opening theme during the opening credits and the ending theme. As for the rest of the soundtrack, it's just a failing pile of trash. Now, let's get to the positive elements in this "film". Yes, surprisingly, this "movie" has some good things in it. All of the sets/locations and the special effects are good. The only thing that almost cost the sets/locations star is that it is in black and white. That just accentuates the boredom of the environment. But, it suits the story, or lack thereof, in this "movie". So, I still give it a pass at the end of the day. Finally, the special effects are good and still hold up to this day. My only nitpick is that all of the words in the opening and closing credits are all lower case. Did a kid write the titles and credits? Or, did someone forget to capitalize? "12 Angry Men" has found a place on my most disappointing films list and most boring films list. It's a real shame, because I really tried so hard to like it. But, it did next to nothing for me. I'm struggling to rate this "film" 2 out of 5 stars on my scale, which equates to 4 out of 10 IMDB stars. Just stay away from "12 Angry Men", it sucks, plain and simple. The sad thing is, that there are schmucks out there who like it, and some even consider it to be their favorite movie! Why? What are you all drinking? God forbid any of you watch an exciting movie, you may have a heart attack! "12 Angry Men" in my verdict is guilty of all charges. All it does is remind me of how much I hate jury duty!

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
For its time, this movie must've been excellent. However, today it holds up as a good older movie that was filmed in black and white with many other older films in its time, shortly before, and shortly after surpassing it. Films such as Casablanca, Vertigo, North by Northwest, Gone With the Wind, Some Like It Hot, Sunset Boulevard, and many others are equally as good for this time period, and some are much better.

While I did appreciate and respect the movie and even liked it, I was very surprised at how high it was ranked on here at number five. There were no major plot twists, surprises, or even tour de force performances that you would also see in some other black and white older films. The concept was very interesting and kept my attention, but even some of the arguments and deductions that the jurors made were not truly logical. Some of them were intelligent, like when Henry Fonda measured the amount of time it would take for the older man witness to walk to the door, as well as when he proved he could purchase the weapon, but overall some of the points made were guesswork.

The truth is that at the end of the day, the director decides to paint Fonda's character as an ideal perfect person while clealry letting the culprit, likely guilty, walk free, which I felt betrayed the script's ambiguity. And to be totally honest, it would have been a much better movie, warranting a ranking of five all-time, if there was a plot twist that one of the juror's arguing for guilt was indeed the actual culrpit- a twist I was waiting and hoping for that I never got. Instead, we get a glorification of Fonda's character to the very end, ironically an antihero that wasn't truly meant to be that allowed the guilty one walk free.

6/10.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
In every which way this movie is overrated aside from maybe the acting and even that I believe is good but not great.

The lone juror who voted not guilty initially (played by Henry Fonda) did so at the time solely on the basis of the fact that he ' 'could possibly ' be not guilty and he just didn't know. That in no way qualifies as not beyond a reasonable doubt. It's become a myth that beyond a reasonable doubt means with 110 % certainty. Saying you don't know with no real basis for it doesn't mean not guilty. Or saying the case was too perfect, so therefore it raised suspicion that he might actually just not be guilty is reckless and irresponsible and yet this character is the protagonist in the story. He did in fact manipulate others very early on based on emotional appeal and not case facts.

Further , the juror goes beyond the evidence presented at the trial and even asks the shop owner about the knife. The juror is going way beyond his responsibility and this would be considered a mistrial. The job of a juror is not to imagine themselves as a defendants lawyer, it's to follow each fact presented.

I understand it's just a movie, but it's also a classic and is deceptive for how a jury should operate. It is so unrealistic that it's just silly.

Another odd thing I couldn't figure out was the non stop bantering about how hot the room was. What was the significance of that? We get it, they all wanted to be out of there. It just came up way too often. Watching them all sweat and work on turning on the fan just was a waste of time.

Lastly, all the characters reminded me of a modern social media comment section with some trying to be civil, some name calling, others yelling at one another. By the end of it, like the characters you want it to be done with. Perhaps that was the point ?

Anyways I just can't see the appeal with this version of the movie or its remake. Plenty of other movies about justice available to watch that are not only more entertaining , but also more realistic.

title: 12 Angry Men
comment:
I'm going to be contrary. The movie is about as preachy as you can get. The 12 jurors are all cartoonish stereotypes, locked into their predictable characters. The unlikeable characters, of course, all make vacuous, absurd arguments for there position, while yelling and gesticulating. The characters we're supposed to like all make calm, reasonable arguments.

The morality is laid out in stark black and white. No grey, no ambiguity, no difficult choices. Me, I like a movie with a dilemma, and some "lesser of two evils" choices. Each character should also be a mixture of good and bad and grey.

Don't you get tired of Hollywood clonking you over the head with a moral lesson? Especially when Hollywood isn't any better than the rest of us.
